items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that a person might like the Cirque shows generally but not like Le Reve, but that's really a separate discussion. To me the theater and design are the best parts. The scenery and stuff around is stunning from start to finish, and the whole concept is lovely. But it doesn't work too well on stage. The plot isn't very interesting. I went to see it once and the stage broke down a lot during the show. That was hard to sit through, even in the better scenes. Le Reve is trying to do the spectacle that Cirque is known for but doesn't quite get there. I think you should only see it if you want to see the nice theater. If not, use the money to see a different show.

I spent 38 dollars on this used mechanical board and I think you get what you pay for, maybe a bit more. The spacebar rattles. Every time I hit it with my thumb it makes a hollow clatter sound, just like knocking around a tray of cutlery. I manage to tune it out during the day but once it is past midnight I notice it every time. The E key also repeats randomly, so typing meeting gives you meeeting, happens maybe once every few paragraphs. Rare enough to forget about but frequent enough that I have to reread everything before sending it. I messaged the seller asking what switches it had, got tired of waiting and bought it anyway. They replied a week later, and I already had it on my desk. Brown switches. The reason I am keeping it is the comfort. Each key has a bump partway down so your fingers know the press registered without slamming to the bottom. I can write a long email and my wrists are fine after. That is something my laptop keys never managed. I thought about sending it back. Return shipping would have eaten a real chunk of the 38 dollars I paid, and I would be back on the laptop. So it stays, rattle and all.

Saw this circus style theatrical production in Vegas. I recommend it. Dropped a star from the review. The story can be hard to follow and some of the music is boring and not fit for the action. The performers are great, impressive athleticism, great physique, great aerobic skills. The women are especially good. They go underwater for several minutes at a time. The theater is circular, stage is circular, so every seat has a good view. There are three stage entrances that are used throughout and during some of the major changes in the story they're very important. The stage, the setting, the lighting are really pretty, beautiful, and it's a very memorable atmosphere. Prices are decent, not as expensive as O and Love for example. I wish they had more spectacular effects, especially fire, but that's not a big deal. The story and the music are not good but it's a fun show and visually really striking. Highly recommend it.

Remote work gets treated like a cure for everything. But two years mentoring 5 juniors made me see its limitations. Juniors still learning to code are not helped much.

They don't need a ticket or a meeting or a document. They need to be in the room for the design talk. They need to watch how others debug stuff. They need to ask questions early, before spending hours stuck. That just happens on its own in an office. On remote, the junior has to know exactly when to jump in or start a call, and also explain an issue they don't quite get yet. That's a hard skill to have before you've actually got the chance to pick it up.

I have seen the problems. On remote, short code review comments feel like the last word, not a chance to learn. It also takes longer, so you lose momentum. The jrs I worked with usually got better faster if they did pairing, whiteboard stuff, etc. and could grab a senior easily.

I am not saying we should all be back in offices or that flexible schedules are no good. Remote work can work great for self-directed developers. For juniors though, being near people builds confidence, context, and gut feel. Sending a junior home with a laptop and a calendar can slow down their growth, which means less good technical leadership further down the line.

It's past three in the morning. The mixer makes a constant humming sound. It's been going for hours, I'm assuming, and it's shaking right through the bottom of my boots. Flour dust fills the air, and the fluorescent light is harsh. It's all like a bunch of snow stuck to the air. The loaves are out on wooden boards and still have a soft crust, they're not fully baked. I wipe my hands off my apron, it's pretty stiff with dried dough and sweat. I check the lock on the door, every day. I know it's not needed, but it's just paranoia.

There's this book, *The History of Salt*. Hardback, blue spine is cracked. It's been here every Thursday for about six weeks, and it's always right on the glass case. Not a library book, we're not part of the city library system. I pick it up, it's cold to the touch. I open it and there's a folded piece of lined paper that falls on the counter. Unfolds it. It's written in rough handwriting, all jagged and pressed hard into the fiber. It says you knead with your left hand dominant, stop using the right hand, it'll ruin the tension. I stare at the words. The mixer ticks over to the next cycle. I look down at my own hands, red knuckles, white dust on them. Close the book. Put it back on the glass, line the spine up with the edge exactly. Then turn off the light over the display.

I think Apple deserves a bit of criticism from my own experience. My school only allowed Apple laptops for middle and high school kids even though they were around double the cost of PC machines. The laptops were breaking down like once a month. Never dropped my laptop once but had to replace the hard drive 5 times in 4 years and reinstalled OS many times. My friend's MacBook Pro caught fire in the middle of a movie and the smoke alarm went off. Apple support was no help, would just back up the machine, wipe it and restore the files. My criticism also extends to iPhones. I owned the first iPhone and it was constantly malfunctioning. Apple release a new iPhone every 2 months or so and it just has a slightly better camera than the previous model. One positive, with a caveat, iPad's are the best tablets out there right now but I think android tablets will catch up eventually.

I'm always in Las Vegas as a kid, we were always going there and have seen a lot of shows, so I've seen plenty of them. I was in Vegas for 21 years. So I think it's okay. It's a good show, but not a must-see show. It's not something I would plan a trip around. But it is okay. One good thing about it is the circular stage. And it's actually really, really good. From pretty much anywhere, you get a good view, which is unusual for a Vegas show. And if you stay at the Wynn or the Encore, it's $99 instead of $125, which is a good deal. But the story is really weak or nonexistent. It's really hard to get a sense of what it's about. And it's just... it's too much. There's too much going on. And it's so loud and so busy. So I don't know. I think that a lot of the individual acts are pretty cool. The performers are really good. The aerialists, the acrobats, and stuff. But it's kind of similar to what you see in a Cirque du Soleil show. And I think that it's really messy, it's just too much. But I don't know. I think it's okay. It's just not something that I would see again. Or pay full price again. And no one really, my friends did enjoy it. But I would say if you have not seen it, you should go see it, especially if you stay at the Wynn. But I don't think I'll be going back. And it's just a really big, flashy show. And more is better, but it's not for me.

First seemed positive, my friend, his little brother and me just chatting with this female manager while she was putting the board together. She said she assembles every day, but one day she was in bad mood and was mean to customers and others. Took 90 mins, but I thought would take 15 or less. Bought a used mechanical keyboard for 38 dollars and its been a mess but its actually kind of cool. The guy who sold it had terrible communication. I asked what switches it had before I bought it and waited a whole week to get back with just one word. By then I had already committed and ordered it. The keyboard itself is super used. The space bar rattles really badly, sounds like a loose Lego brick or something. The E key randomly double types sometimes, so I am writing theee instead of the. Funny. But even with the flaws I really enjoy typing on this board. Tactile feel is great, very comfortable for writing long annoying work emails. I thought about sending it back but returning a heavy chunk of plastic that cost 38 dollars is too much hassle. So I kept it and have grown fond of the flaws. If you are okay with some do it yourself fixes and a letter typing twice now and then its a good deal for the price.

Turkish Airlines really messed me over. Harbin to Beijing got delayed, so I missed my connection to Istanbul. Went to the Turkish desk at airport, and no one took the blame or rebooked me. I had to sleep in the airport. Next morning, I asked for a ticket. They said flights were overbooked and it could take days to get to Istanbul unless I paid for business class. I needed to get to Istanbul, so I paid for business class. I can't believe it.

You bring just one broken item for repair. Walk up to the desk when you arrive and get a numbered ticket. That number is your turn in the line, keep it safe. Volunteers who know the stuff fix things on a first come first served basis. Need to pick up your item before the volunteers go home at 4 pm. If you don't grab it, they won't store it overnight. Make sure you've got enough time to wait. They can't promise to fix every device. Thanks for following these procedures, helps keep the whole thing running smoothly.

A float valve controls the trough. A float is connected to a valve. When the water level drops, the float sinks and opens the valve, letting water in. As the water rises, the float rises and slowly closes the valve. When it reaches the set level, the valve stops and filling stops. I think it's easy to overflow. Either debris, or the minerals on the valve stop it from closing, or the float is set too high, so the valve closes only after the trough is already overflowing.

Went to this place Sunday at 7:20 because we had a show at the same hotel at 10 and thought it would be convenient. Never actually ate. Put names on the useless digital list and they said come back to pay at 8:23. We did and just stood about 15 minutes before staff said we probably wouldn't be sat until 9:15. Just two people. No help offered. If you're going to wait way past payment you should just say so up front, or at least give options instead of leaving us to find them. Wasted night. Would be zero stars if I could give them.

Dear Enron staff,

I know things are a bit rough. What is going on inside Enron and then the bad news out in the world, it doesn't feel festive at all. We had long discussions on the party on 8 December. Some people wanted to go ahead with it, to celebrate. Others thought it was not right now. We made the call that we would cancel. I know how this may be received. Spending company money to celebrate in such times doesn't feel prudent. I'm sorry. You have worked hard. You deserve to be recognised and celebrated. We will find other more appropriate ways to recognise your hard work over the holiday season.

Ken Lay

Water goes from one container to another in a siphon, moving over something higher. What makes it work is gravity plus the air pressure, just like in your lungs. To get it going, you have to start with water in the whole tube, so there is one unbroken column. The longer end of the tube will have gravity pulling down toward the lower container. This downward move makes the pressure near the top of the siphon drop. Air pressure is pushing down on the water level of the source container, so it forces liquid up the shorter tube to fill the low pressure spot, and that's what keeps it flowing.

The outlet needs to be lower than the water level in the starting container. The force really comes from the difference in water weight in the two tube ends. If the outlet is even with the water level or higher, then gravity isn't pulling down hard enough to lift it up on the intake side. There isn't a gravitational net pull unless the tube end that is lower has more water weight than the tube end that is rising.

When air gets into the tube, the continuous column of water gets broken. Air bubbles mess up the chain of water molecules and stop the pull from being transmitted. So the pressure equalizes between the tube and the outside air. And once that happens, the flow stops. The whole thing doesn't work until you fill the tube up with water again.

The sourdough was in its second rise. Again. So it always happens on Thursdays, right on the flour bin, and again the same book, Monte Cristo, with the Richmond Public Library stamp on it. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing them, but at 3 AM I'm basically just yeast and caffeine and no real brain to hear anything. Except this time, there was a piece of yellow legal pad paper sticking out of the top, like a bookmark. So I wiped my hands on my apron and pulled the note out. It said page 142. And please. The handwriting is really spiky. It says I think they're watching the drop box now. A cold draft came through the kitchen, wet asphalt smell, rain coming. I looked at the front windows. Just saw my own reflection, tired, staring back. Didn't open the book. But tucked the note back in and slid the novel into a brown pastry bag and folded the top down twice.

Got a used mechanical keyboard off someone for 38 dollars. I think i got 38 dollars worth or a little more. So first off, its flaws. The space bar rattles. Not a nice click but this loose clatter when i hit it. During the day i stopped noticing but late at night it's really loud. The e key will repeat itself and i type meeeting or something once in a while. Happens every few paragraphs, enough that i have to check my text. The seller was slow to respond. I asked what switches it had, got a reply a week later, which was after the keyboard was already here. Brown switches. And the good part, it is actually really comfortable. Nice cushy keys, can write long emails without my wrists hurting. My laptop before had a really flat keyboard that was not as good. I thought about returning it but it did not seem worth the hassle. So its staying on my desk, rattling and repeating, and quietly doing its job. Three stars

Hi everyone. I'm Tom's sibling, not sure which one. He shared my bunk bed until he was 14, so I know him in a fairly close kind of way. I remember him snoring. I remember him arguing over who got the top bunk. These are things that show you pretty quickly the person he is. He's a very reliable guy. We are celebrating that today. I can count on him. I once forgot my passport. He had to drive for 6 hours to bring it to me. He's a loyal brother, he's generous. He'll go out of his way to save you from your own idiocy. It's unreasonable distances and stuff. So, Tom, I'm very happy you found someone who loves you like us. But, unlike me, you're rooming with them on a voluntary basis.

I never really wanted to see a Cirque show until now. Le Reve was my first. I imagined lots of backflips and crazy acrobatics. And it had less of that than I thought. It was more interpretive dancing and not just the tumbling. So it's very different from what I had in mind. The talent is clearly there, but it is not my thing. If you really like this kind of theatre I think you will enjoy it. For me it's not something I would spend over $100 on. I went on free tickets. I'm very happy I got in for free.

Old attendance registers really help historians work out how people actually lived day to day, stuff that's often missing from official accounts. They list which kids came to school and which didn't, how often, and sometimes why they missed. From that you can work out things like seasonal work, sickness, bad weather, money worries, looking after family, moving to another place, or something happening locally. They can also show what varied by age, class, or which corner of town kids came from. That helps us see how education fitted in with work and running the household. Over a long period, it shows habits of schooling changed and public health. The catch is that registers only say what the school recorded. They don't really talk about what kids were going through. Missing from school might be wrong, patchy, or just down to what teachers assumed. So you're best off cross-checking them with other records.

Every Thursday at 2:17, Mara spots the same library book on the bakery's back step. Its county sticker is faded, and there is flour in the cover, looks like the book was helping with the work. She returned it twice, but the librarians just smiled politely. On week three she stopped complaining and kept it next to the rye starter. Tonight the rain was tapping the alley door. The ovens running hot, she was pressing butter into croissant dough, when the back latch clicked open. Nobody there, just the book sitting dry on wet concrete. She wiped her hands and opened it. A note was folded once, tucked between the Luna Moth and Promethea pages. It read: your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. Apologies for the crumbs. Looking out at the alley, the dented milk crates, steam off the drains, she felt the city was big for a moment, then not so big. She tore off the corner of an order pad and wrote that cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. She put the note back inside the book, set it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

This project used cardboard bridges to compare folded designs. Students made a short beam, an arch inspired one, and a triangular fold with the same cardboard, tried to keep the size same. They set up the bridges between two supports and put weights on little by little to see if they bent, tipped or fell over. The study was limited, because the bridges were hand made and there were not many trials and classroom conditions. So the results should not be taken as real engineering data. In the end, the triangular fold ones held weights steadier. So we can tell that fold shape matters on how a model bridge stays stable.

Marguerite saw the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. It was called *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. Inside the cover the Harbor Street library branch stamp said it was due back in March. The mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago. Next to it there was the hatch the flour guy used. That one didn't ever latch right.

Eleven Thursdays. She had asked the day staff. She looked for scratches in the hatch. Once she stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book showed up between two and four. And she was always at the ovens, back turned to the door, when it did.

Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded up on the oystercatcher page. The ink had gone blotchy where someone pressed hard.

*I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.*

She thought whoever wrote it smelled of salt. The pages did. Marguerite pulled a pencil out of her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt. *Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll.* She tucked it in at the oystercatchers, put the book on the hatch ledge and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

ive moved to Toronto so i dont use hydro ottawa anymore but i feel people need to hear about their weird billing stuff. when i was renting downtown i had an account for a year. moved back in with my parents for my masters and cancelled properly and paid off what i owed. but even after cancelling they kept taking money out of a different bank account i had on random dates for more than a year. i called and sent over proof of the charges, every time the people on the other line would say my account was closed and no more payments were happening. it only got figured out when my parents and i went through the bills together. the banking info had gotten tied to their bill number just because i said im staying with them. they hadnt really noticed since they always got money back as overpayment refunds, so the extra credit seemed normal. i sat on the phone hours at a stretch with people in different departments. a manager took a proper look and got it fixed. what i find nuts is they first said no refund. just an apology. i will not ever again put my banking info for autodebit, this is what happens to our info, and it really should be concerning.

It was 3:40 am. Second batch of rye was proofing. Marisol found the book again. It was leaning on the flour bin by the back door, still cold from the alley. This was the fourth Thursday it came back. The book was a field guide to night birds, from the Eastgate Branch library, and the due date was three weeks past. Every Thursday she carried it to the drop box on her way home, but Thursday after Thursday it returned, as if the building had borrowed it. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. There was a folded index card stuck to the barn owl page. It read: you leave the vent fan on, and the alley smells like bread until 5. She walks her mother's dog now because the mother can't anymore. She keeps forgetting to return this, maybe she just doesn't want to. Signed R. She read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark. She turned the card over. Using the grease pencil she uses for marking trays, she wrote rye's out at 4:15. Then she tore a heel off yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, put the book on top, and propped the back door open just an inch.

I went with Ryanair while I was broke as a student. Ex lived in Sweden and they were just the cheapest. The whole thing was terrible. At the airport they took my 20 pound L'Occitane shower gel and claimed it was over the liquid limit but it wasn't. Said I could get it back if I went to the pharmacy to buy a 100ml bottle. So I did exactly that. Came back, nobody knew what I was on about. Brilliant. Lost my twenty quid, absolutely furious. They also charged me another five pounds at the gate. I had a water bottle in my hand luggage, which I bought at the airport. Ryanair stopped flying Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta, so now I fly Norwegian. Their customer service is bad too, ironically, but the planes feel newer and less old fashioned than Ryanair's.

Not just you, i got caught in a really heavy rain on tuesday and by thursday half my brandywines had split. Can see the seam running down the side. Its the old story of dry then sudden deluge. inside takes water faster than skin can stretch. Sungolds mostly holding up but a few look like they might follow.
Nothing really to do once weather happens. only helps to keep your two day schedule more even. but does not really matter once sky lets it all out at once. youll probably get a decent crop off the rest. just pick off the split ones and put them to other uses.
much more of a pain with brandywines. the thick skin is a real liability in this kind of storm. you might have better luck with sungolds if you can keep them from getting as much water at once.

The College Board makes no bones about being two faced. My friend sat a one hour SAT subject test but the proctor made a mistake and gave the room about 20 extra minutes. Being honest, she knew the test was standardised and this advantage meant it wasn't fair, so she reported it on the official hotline to stop future mess-ups. And the results were just wrong. They did some kind of investigation then said there wasn't enough evidence to punish the proctor or other students. But what is really ridiculous is they said there was enough evidence against my friend to cancel her scores. So they punish the person who spoke up and let the people who actually messed it up off the hook. It just goes to show how unfair and broken the whole organisation is.

The book always appears on Thursday. No one puts it on the counter, it ends up behind the flour bins by the back door. Whoever leaves it seems to have a very specific place for it, somewhere I'm unlikely to trip on it. And it's always the same book, A Field Guide to North American Moths from Elmwood branch. The due date stamp is so old it's purple. I've never seen anyone return it. By 2pm I'm up to my elbows in rye dough and at that time of day I wouldn't see a marching parade. The first few weeks I'd just leave it on the shelf next to the till. Then by Friday it's gone, and it's back again Thursday. All right. People are odd. I talk to my sourdough starter so I'm not one to judge. Tonight there was a note in it, on page 114, the luna moth page. It was written in pencil, pressed hard. No signature. It says, they only live for a week, and they don't even eat, it's a waste of a beautiful thing, and does one ever get to see the bread before it's gone. I read it three times, first and second time, then once more as the ovens ticked. Then I got the first loaf of the night out, still crackling, wrapped in brown paper, put it behind the flour bins.

My room feels muggy even when it's a nice temperature. Humidity is a real problem. When it's high, your sweat doesn't dry well. Air sits there. Air doesn't move. So the fumes, smells, CO2, heat, all stay right there. Ventilation is bad. Air conditioning may cool the air, but it doesn't necessarily dry it out or move it. Opening a window, a fan, and ventilation will help move it around. That will help with the humidity. That will help the stuffy feel.

Remote work is sold as everyone wins. I mentored five junior engineers over the past two years and it's not really true. They don't need tickets, or docs or scheduled meetings. What they do need is being in the design arguments, watching another person work through a nasty bug, and getting answers before a little bit of uncertainty turns into a big problem. You get all of that for free if you're in the office. Working from home they have to figure out when to interrupt someone and get a call set up and explain a problem they probably don't even understand yet. That is pretty steep for someone who hasn't had a chance to learn it.

I have seen that setup really mess up feedback. A short note on a code review ends up sounding like a final judgment. The lag on getting answers kills any forward motion. The ones I worked with made a lot more progress when they could pair in person, work through things on a whiteboard and actually get hold of the seniors. None of this means throw out flexibility. It works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there. That is how they pick up the confidence and context and judgment they need. You'll end up with weaker technical leadership later on if you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar.

A rain gauge is simple. Rain falls into an opening of known area and the result is reported as depth, typically mm or inches. This depth means how much water would cover flat ground if none is lost to run-off, evaporation or soak. Many gauges have a funnel with a wide opening that feeds a thin tube. Same amount of water rises higher in a thin tube so small quantities are easier to read. The tube has a scale adjusted for the area ratio so you still get true rainfall depth. Wind is a common error. Gusts blow rain past the opening so you under count. Also you get distortion of results from evaporation or splash before you read it.

Paid 38 quid second hand, pulled it out and the price was fine, just some dust between keys, some shiny bits on the caps, no worse than expected from a used thing. I write long emails for work, and it's more comfortable for me, my hands are less cramped compared to my flat office one. The switches feel quite steady, not too heavy, the base doesn't slide around. The problem is the spacebar, every time I hit it it rattles, very loud in the morning, and the E key repeats sometimes, so if I type too fast I'll get things like neeed, it doesn't happen all the time but it happens enough that I have to proofread more carefully. I asked the seller what switches they were and they took a full week to reply after it had already arrived. Not great, but for 38 I kept it. Shipping it back felt like more hassle than it was worth.

Ok, so its 1 item per person, come see the volunteers at the front table. They will number your ticket, keep it until they return your item. The volunteers will call out numbers, and you should stay close by because sometimes your input is needed. Not all items will be fixable, sometimes parts need to be ordered, sometimes its not possible. So you need to come collect your item before 4:30 when the volunteers leave, and if they don't see you, they won't be storing it.

Went on a Friday at around 4:30 p.m. and to my surprise nobody else was there, so zero wait. Two of us spent about $130 total. I went in thinking it would cost about the same as a good steakhouse, but afterwards I found out it actually cost more than I expected to pay at one. The fact that they didn't do steak honestly let me down. For that price I assumed at least one steak option would be there. They had lamb, prime rib, and chicken. Those are meats you can get at other Vegas buffets for a lot less. The seafood bit had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. The Alaskan legs are everywhere, but rock claws I hadn't seen elsewhere, which was cool. However there was no crackers for the claws. They said wooden mallets were available, but our table was very close to the next one and I did not feel like smashing shells and sending fragments flying at the people next to us. I just ate the legs. The Asian station was not all that special. Reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. For dessert, they had gelato and pastries, but nothing really jumped out. They had fresh juice, I didn't try it. I'd call it acceptable, but it is overpriced for what they offer. If you are curious, try it once if there is no wait. But if the line is long, I might reconsider.

The old school attendance books are great for historians who want to see how life in a community actually ran. These books recorded which kids showed up each day. If a large number of students stopped coming, it could have been an outbreak of flu or a harvest time when the kids needed to help their families with work. This shows the struggle between going to school and needing to work. We also see that some groups of kids stopped coming for long stretches. This can suggest social gaps or how different cultures felt about education. The problem is that teachers or headmasters might have changed numbers to look good to the authorities. Or maybe they wanted to get money. So the numbers are not always right. These books hardly ever tell us why a kid is absent. The researcher has to compare it with other sources to guess what happened. So we get to know numbers, but for social structure and daily life, you have to cross-check everything.

I am using personal experience on this, Apple has to be mentioned. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high schoolers, and they cost twice as much as other options and broke roughly every month. I never dropped my laptop once but had the hard drive replaced 5 times in 4 years and reinstalled the OS many times just to keep it running. A friend's MacBook Pro caught fire during a movie, which set off the smoke alarm. Apple support never diagnosed anything, just backed up, wiped and restored. Same story with iPhones. I had the first iPhone and it was always malfunctioning. Apple release a new iPhone every 2 months, with just a slightly better camera than the last model. Ive just had a trough that overflowed badly. The float valve connects trough to water line and its under pressure. Its got a plastic ball or a block on the water, hooked up to a lever arm, and it goes up and down with the level. When the cows drink, the level goes down, float sinks, and the arm tilts and pulls the plunger or washer off the valve seat and water comes in. And its the same thing, as the water goes up the float lifts up, lever pushes plunger back against the seat, and it starts closing off. And the overflow thing. So if the washer gets worn or gets dirt or bits in it, its not getting a good seal. Or the float gets a hole in it and fills with water so its not lifting enough to close off the valve.
